Moist
moist
adj. (fresh, not dried; of grapes, unripened into raisins)
From the Old French moiste, damp. In Scripture it occurs once, in the law of the Nazarite, where the separated man is cut off from the vine in every form it can take.

Biblical Definition

The law of separation is exhaustive about the vine: “He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried” (Numbers 6:3). Moist grapes are fresh grapes; dried grapes are raisins; and between the two the statute has closed every door. The vow it belongs to is defined at the outset: “Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When either man or woman shall separate themselves to vow a vow of a Nazarite, to separate themselves unto the LORD” (Numbers 6:2). The thoroughness continues to the plant itself: “All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk” (Numbers 6:4). And the reason for the whole apparatus is given without embarrassment: “All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD” (Numbers 6:8). The law is not squeamish about grapes; Scripture elsewhere calls wine a gift that makes glad the heart of man. The point of forbidding a lawful good is that the abstaining itself is the sign. A Nazarite walking past a vineyard was a visible sentence about who owned his days.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines moist as moderately wet; damp; and applies it to fruit not dried.

expand to see more

MOIST, a. Moderately wet; damp; as, a moist atmosphere or air.

NAZARITE, n. A Jew who professed extraordinary purity of life and devotion, and bound himself by a vow of separation.

SEPARATE, v.t. To disunite; to divide; to set apart for a particular purpose or use.

VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a solemn promise, by which a person binds himself to do or forbear something.

ABSTINENCE, n. In general, the act or practice of voluntarily refraining from the use of something.

Key Scripture

Numbers 6:3 — "He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried."

Numbers 6:2 — "Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When either man or woman shall separate themselves to vow a vow of a Nazarite, to separate themselves unto the LORD:"

Numbers 6:4 — "All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk."

Numbers 6:8 — "All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Voluntary abstinence is either dismissed as legalism or inflated into a mark of superior holiness, and the Nazarite's actual purpose — a visible sign of separation unto the LORD — is lost between the two errors.

expand to see more

Two opposite corruptions attach to this statute. The first, common wherever Christian liberty is prized more than it is understood, reads the Nazarite vow as the sort of scrupulosity the gospel abolished, and treats any voluntary abstaining as a return to bondage. The text does not support the caricature. The vow was temporary, voluntary, available to man or woman, and ended with a sacrifice and a haircut — the Nazarite went back to the vineyard. It was never a higher tier of Israelite; it was a season with a sign attached.

The opposite corruption is the older one, and the church has suffered more from it: abstinence treated as intrinsic merit, the abstainer as further along, the refusal of a lawful good as itself a virtue. Paul names this error directly when he writes of those forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving. The Nazarite gave up moist grapes and dried ones not because grapes are unclean but because separation needed a visible shape. Where the sign is mistaken for the holiness, the vow has become the thing the Reformers called will-worship.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lach (H3892), fresh or moist; nazir (H5139), a Nazarite, one separated; nazar (H5144), to separate; qadosh (H6918), holy.

expand to see more

Hebrew lach (H3892) — fresh, moist, green; the moist grapes of Numbers 6:3.

Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated, a Nazarite; the same root as an untrimmed vine.

Hebrew nazar (H5144) — to separate, consecrate oneself unto the LORD.

Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow, a voluntary promise made to God.

Hebrew qadosh (H6918) — holy, set apart; he is holy unto the LORD.

Usage

"“Nor eat moist grapes, or dried” — the vine closed off in every form."

"“From the kernels even to the husk” — the thoroughness of the separation."

"“He is holy unto the LORD” — the purpose of the whole statute."
